text.content:
Perception, interruption and movement

Player rolls — agreed

When a player looks for something, the DA calls for Reason, with Boons/Banes for circumstances. When someone might perceive a hidden player character, that player rolls Agility to remain Hidden. Do not add an opposed observer roll. Ordinary obvious information requires no roll. Hidden remains universal; actual concealment and a plausible approach matter.

Procedure: active searching or attempting to hide during combat costs a Main Action unless a card states otherwise. A hidden creature that attacks or openly reveals itself loses Hidden. No roll conceals someone in plain view with no plausible concealment. Establish progress and consequences before an unscripted roll. A Weak search might narrow the location; a Weak hiding attempt might reach cover while leaving evidence. These examples do not override the scene or a card’s printed outcomes.

Opportunities — agreed

Starting a provoking action triggers the opportunity attack before that action resolves. Resolve Basic Melee using the attacker’s normal player-roll procedure; no specialty attack. Then the original action continues if its actor is still capable; otherwise it stops. Damage alone does not automatically cancel the action. Forced movement never provokes.

Leaving melee reach voluntarily, casting a spell beside an enemy, standing, stowing and retrieving items are the intended triggers established in discussion. Drawing as part of an attack stays part of that attack. Timing: commit the action when declared; check targets and capability again after interruption; pay an additional printed HP/item cost only when continuing into its resolution. If interrupted permanently, the committed action is spent but an unspent potion or HP cost is not consumed.

Player-controlled creatures — agreed

Creature cards must print attack and defense attributes. The controlling player rolls those printed creature attributes, not their character’s attribute. When an NPC attacks a player-controlled summon, its controller rolls the summon’s defense. When the summon attacks, its controller makes the attack roll. Use the ordinary single-roll attack/defense outcome mapping. A player-controlled attacker does not also cause a second player defense roll.

A summon disappears when its controller becomes unconscious or dies. An uncommanded summon does nothing; existing effects and conditions still resolve.

NPC-only resolution — approved October 16, 2026

Either a player or the DA assuming the player role can roll for NPC-only actions. For an NPC attacking another NPC, roll the defending NPC’s printed attribute named by the attack, with the applicable modifiers. Read the attacking creature’s Weak / Standard / Strong defense outcomes. Make only one roll, not an opposed pair.

For consequential NPC healing or another task, the same choice of roller uses the acting NPC’s printed attribute and outcomes. This does not transfer control of the NPC to the person handling the dice. Existing player-character and player-controlled creature procedures remain unchanged.

For example, when a bandit attacks an allied guard with an Agility-defense attack, a player or the DA rolls the guard’s Agility defense and reads the bandit’s card. Off-screen events may be resolved by DA judgment without rolling through unseen combat.

Stability and ordinary movement

Stability — approved: all characters and creatures start at 0; only an explicit trait, ability or item raises it, maximum 3, highest source only. It consumes forced movement once for the initial target and once for each new creature struck in a collision chain. Stop when movement is exhausted; never charge a creature twice. It does not resist Prone, grapples or conditions. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.5ebfaad0d5ed6813.JournalEntryPage.3292b6a49dcf7236]{Stability} for a worked example. Collision timing approved October 16, 2026: resolve contact collision damage from movement remaining on arrival, then deduct the new member’s Stability before further travel. Applicable resistance still reduces damage.

Agreed: falling deals 3 HP per 2 squares fallen. Rounding and damage: use 3 × floor(distance / 2), physical damage with ordinary physical resistance; falls under 2 squares deal no automatic damage. Exceptional landing surfaces and circumstances are DA rulings.

Agreed: climbing and swimming use difficult-terrain movement cost, normally 2 per square, unless an ability changes it. Impossible surfaces and impassable currents do not become traversable merely by spending movement. Roll only when uncertainty has consequences. Cards can improve the ordinary activity.

Jumping — approved: broad jump up to max(1, 2 + Agility) squares; high jump up to max(0, 1 + floor(Agility / 2)) squares. Each square traveled spends movement; a broad jump needs 2 squares of approach, otherwise halve its maximum, rounded down (minimum 1). A high jump needs no approach. Land in a legal supported free square; no extra movement or passage through barriers. Negative Agility can mean no full square of high-jump clearance, not inability to hop over a small obstacle. Obstacles below a square and risky landings are adjudicated normally. No roll for a clear, safe jump within these limits; risky execution can call for Agility. These values are approved; specialist movement cards retain their explicit exceptions.

Consequence vocabulary

A consequence is what is at stake: harm, lost time, exposure, lost supplies, a worsened position or an opportunity that closes. A complication introduces an additional problem while retaining whatever progress the roll achieved. A benefit adds a useful advantage. State the stakes before rolling. Weak is progress, not automatic success; Strong is success with the printed result. Natural 111 adds a complication to Weak; 666 adds a benefit to Strong.

Use 1 Bane for a meaningful obstacle, 2 for a severe obstacle, 3 for an exceptional obstacle that remains possible. Use Boons symmetrically for real help or advantageous circumstances. These are DA guidance bands, not target numbers. Cancel Boons/Banes and apply the existing net cap of 3. Do not roll impossible attempts or apply the same obstacle twice under different names. Group progress and binary/cumulative task targets keep their existing rules.

Magic boundaries — agreed

Countermagic uses defensive interference and disruption; a separate generic spell cancellation system is not required. Healing used against a healing-harmed unwilling creature resolves as an attack spell, like Flame Dart: use the spell’s printed attribute and result as Life damage, normal attack targeting and resistance. Keep the healing spell’s action, range, free hand and upfront life cost. Beneficial recovery riders do not help that target. Eligible creature cards must print the appropriate defense attribute; no extra opposed save is added. Ordinary willing healing retains its existing procedure.
